steps.explain: Dot product with \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\underset{\sim}{a}\). Use \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=|\underset{\sim}{a}|^{2}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\cos\angle AOB\); then \(|\underset{\sim}{b}|=|\underset{\sim}{a}|\) (rhombus).
Dot product with \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\underset{\sim}{b}\), in the same way.
(1) and (2) are equal. Write each dot product with the angle formula \(\underset{\sim}{u}\cdot\underset{\sim}{v}=|\underset{\sim}{u}||\underset{\sim}{v}|\cos\theta\).
Cancel \(|\overrightarrow{OC}|\) and \(|\underset{\sim}{a}|=|\underset{\sim}{b}|\) (non-zero).
Both angles are between \(0^{\circ}\) and \(180^{\circ}\), where cosine is one-to-one, so the angles are equal: \(OC\) bisects \(\angle AOB\) (green and orange arcs).

Why not the others: B only shows the diagonals are perpendicular; C is a statement, not a proof; D skips the step that turns equal dot products into equal angles (it needs \(|\underset{\sim}{a}|=|\underset{\sim}{b}|\) and the range of the angles).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: If \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are two non-zero vectors on the Cartesian plane, which of the following statements is NOT ALWAYS CORRECT ?
questions.hint: The length of proj_v u is |u||cos θ|. Which statement compares it with the wrong vector?

steps.explain: The projection of \(\mathbf u\) onto \(\mathbf v\) is the 'shadow' of \(\mathbf u\) on the line of \(\mathbf v\). Its length is \(|\mathbf u||\cos\theta|\le|\mathbf u|\), so A is always true.
The signed length is \(\mathbf u\cdot\hat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|}\), so C and D are always true.
B compares with the length of \(\mathbf v\), which has nothing to do with the shadow. Counterexample: \(\mathbf u=2\mathbf i+2\mathbf j\), \(\mathbf v=\mathbf i\).
So B is not always correct.

keyPoints.note: Look for the statement that can fail: try a long u and a short v.

steps.explain: Write the formula for the vector projection of \(p\) onto \(q\).
Calculate the dot product.
Calculate \(|q|^{2}\) (squared length, so no square root is needed).
